hero.title: Apple
hero.desc: Founded April 1, 1976 on Crist Drive in Los Altos by Steve Jobs, Steve Wozniak, and Ronald Wayne. Forty-nine years later the same company sells nearly a billion handheld computers a year and is, by market value, the largest single business in human history.

spotlight.title: iPhone
spotlight.desc: The handheld computer that redefined consumer electronics. Launched in 2007 — 18 years and 3 billion units later, Apple's most defining product and the largest single-revenue product line in human history.

overview.heading: A company built on the bitten apple, the bezier curve, and the relentless deletion of anything that doesn't ship.
paragraphs: Apple Inc. is an American technology company headquartered in Cupertino, California. It designs and sells consumer electronics, computer software, online services, and — since 2020 — its own silicon. The company is structured around vertical integration across hardware, software, and services, a model Steve Jobs called "the whole widget."

Apple's history splits cleanly into five eras. The founding period (1976–1985) produced the Apple I, II, and the original 1984 Macintosh. The wilderness years (1985–1997) saw three CEOs and a billion-dollar loss. The restoration (1997–2007) brought the iMac, OS X, and the iPod. The iPhone era (2007–2011) reshaped consumer electronics globally. The Cook era (2011–present) made Apple the first company to cross $1T, $2T, and $3T in market capitalisation.

events.title: App Store launches.
events.preview: 500 apps. The 2G ships into a live ecosystem — and unlike 1st gen owners, pays nothing to access it.
events.body: Apple’s App Store opened alongside iPhone OS 2.0, transforming the iPod touch from a fixed-feature device into a software platform. At launch, approximately 500 apps were available. For iPod touch 1st generation owners, accessing the App Store required a $9.95 paid software update. The 2nd generation, launching two months later, shipped with App Store access built in at no charge. By the time the 2G went on sale, the store had already recorded 60 million downloads.

events.title: iPod touch 2G unveiled.
events.preview: Contoured stainless back. Speaker. Volume buttons. Nike+. Ships same day at $229, $299, $399.
events.body:
At the Yerba Buena Center for the Arts in San Francisco, Apple introduced the 2nd generation iPod touch at its “Let’s Rock” keynote. A contoured, polished stainless steel back replaced the flat aluminum of the original, tapering toward the edges. Physical volume buttons appeared on the left edge for the first time. A mono speaker sat behind a grille at the top. Nike+iPod support was built in natively.

The device shipped the same day it was announced — running iPhone OS 2.1.1 out of the box, with full App Store access. Pricing was $229 (8GB), $299 (16GB), and $399 (32GB).

events.title: iPhone OS 2.2.
events.preview: Street View in Maps. Transit routing. Podcast downloads over WiFi.
events.body: iPhone OS 2.2 was the first significant update the 2G received after launch. Google Street View was integrated into Maps. Public transit routing was added. Podcast downloading came to the iTunes app, letting users subscribe and receive episodes over WiFi without syncing to a computer.

events.title: 20 million iPod touches sold.
events.preview: Holiday demand for the 2G cited as the primary driver. A market validated fast.
events.body: Apple publicly announced that cumulative iPod touch sales had reached 20 million units worldwide. The 2nd generation model was credited as the primary driver of that demand surge — the redesigned form factor and native App Store access had significantly broadened the device’s appeal.

events.title: iPhone OS 3.0 previewed.
events.preview: Bluetooth unlocked — the chip was always there, silently waiting.
events.body: At Apple’s campus in Cupertino, the company previewed iPhone OS 3.0. Among the announcements specific to the 2G: the update would unlock Bluetooth functionality — not by adding new hardware, but by enabling a Samsung/Broadcom chip that had been present inside the device from launch, silently dormant.

events.title: iPhone OS 3.0 ships.
events.preview: Cut, copy, paste. Bluetooth gaming. Costs iPod touch users $9.95.
events.body: iPhone OS 3.0 was released as a free update for iPhone users. iPod touch owners were charged $9.95. Apple cited Sarbanes-Oxley accounting rationale. On the 2G, the update delivered cut, copy, and paste, Spotlight search, peer-to-peer Bluetooth gaming, and parental controls.

events.title: Lineup revised. MC model arrives.
events.preview: 16GB and 32GB discontinued. Revised 8GB MC at $199 patches the BootROM exploit.
events.body: Apple permanently discontinued the original 16GB and 32GB iPod touch 2G models. In their place, Apple introduced a revised 8GB model — the “MC” series (MC086LL/A) — distinguishable from the original “MB” line by an updated BootROM that patched a hardware-level jailbreak exploit. The revised model shipped at $199 with iPhone OS 3.1 pre-installed.

events.title: iPhone OS 3.1.3.
events.preview: The last update the 2G runs without performance degradation.
events.body: iPhone OS 3.1.3 brought minor bug fixes and security patches. For the 2G specifically, it is widely regarded as the final software version the device ran without meaningful performance degradation — the hardware’s 128MB of RAM and ARMv6 processor were still adequate at this version.

events.title: iOS 4.0 — free, but limited.
events.preview: First free major upgrade. No multitasking, no wallpapers. Hardware ceiling reached.
events.body: Apple released iOS 4.0 — the first time a major version upgrade was delivered to iPod touch users free of charge. Because the 2G featured only 128MB of RAM and an older ARMv6 processor, it could not support multitasking, custom home screen wallpapers, or Bluetooth keyboard support.

events.title: iPod touch 2G discontinued.
events.preview: The 8GB MC model pulled. Entire 2nd generation family ends production.
events.body: On September 1, 2010, Apple removed the iPod touch 2nd generation 8GB MC model from sale, ending production for the entire 2nd generation family. Software support continued for another fourteen months.

events.title: iOS 4.2.1 — the final OS.
events.preview: Game Center. AirPlay audio. The last software this hardware will ever run.
events.body: iOS 4.2.1 served as the final operating system for the iPod touch 2nd generation. It brought Game Center, AirPlay audio streaming, and on-device playlist creation. The limitations remained: no multitasking, no wallpapers, no Bluetooth keyboard.

events.title: iOS 4.3 drops the 2G.
events.preview: Device absent from the compatibility list. Official support ends permanently.
events.body: Apple released iOS 4.3 on March 9, 2011, and the iPod touch 2nd generation was entirely absent from the device compatibility list. This was the formal end of software support. App Store applications requiring iOS 4.3 or later were immediately inaccessible.

events.title: End of life. 60M units.
events.preview: Total iPod touch sales surpass 60 million. The 2G was the primary driver.
events.body: As the 2nd generation reached true end-of-life status, Apple’s metrics showed total iPod touch sales across all generations had surpassed 60 million units worldwide. The 2nd generation had been the primary driver of adoption.

data.heading:
What changed.
1st → 2nd generation.
data.intro: The iPod touch 2nd generation was not a reinvention of the first — it was a completion of it. Every significant gap in the original was addressed: the missing speaker, the missing volume buttons, the recessed headphone jack, the external Nike+ receiver, the flat back that didn’t sit well in the hand. On the software side, the 2G shipped into a live App Store with 60 million downloads already recorded, with access included free on day one — no paid upgrade required.

data.heading:
Four SKUs. One finish.
Only storage differs.
intro: The iPod touch 2nd generation was sold in a single finish — polished stainless steel with a black front bezel — across four distinct SKUs. At launch in September 2008, three storage tiers were available: 8 GB, 16 GB, and 32 GB, priced at $229, $299, and $399 respectively. Every unit shared the same processor, RAM, display, speaker, Nike+ wireless, and battery.

All three launch models were discontinued simultaneously in September 2009, replaced by a single revised 8 GB "MC" model at a new entry price of $199. The revision patched a hardware-level jailbreak exploit and shipped with iPhone OS 3.1 pre-installed.

body.text: The iPod touch 2nd generation launched in September 2008 — two months after the App Store opened with 500 applications. Games were the dominant category from the start, and the 2G was the first iPod touch to ship with native App Store access. Where the 1st generation had been a music player that could browse the web, the 2nd generation arrived as a pocket gaming console that happened to play music.

The timing was structurally significant. The 2G’s 3.5-inch multi-touch display, built-in accelerometer, and responsive capacitive screen made it a natural fit for the wave of touch-native games that defined the App Store’s first year: Tap Tap Revenge, Fieldrunners, Rolando, Flight Control. These were not ports of console games — they were designed from scratch for a touchscreen, and the iPod touch was the cheapest way to play them.

Apple recognized this quickly. By 2009, the company’s marketing had shifted to position the iPod touch explicitly as a gaming device. The “Funnest iPod ever” campaign ran television spots showing games, not music. Steve Jobs showed game demos at keynote events. In multiple quarters between 2008 and 2010, iPod touch unit sales exceeded those of the Nintendo DS and Sony PSP.

The absence of a cellular contract was the key. The iPhone cost $199 plus a two-year AT&T commitment at $60–100 per month. The iPod touch 2G cost $229 with no recurring cost. It introduced a generation of users to the concept that a pocket-sized touchscreen could be a primary gaming device — a market category that did not meaningfully exist before the App Store.

body.text: In 2008, the iPhone was not a mass-market device. It required an AT&T contract — the only carrier that sold it — at a minimum monthly cost of roughly $70. Over two years, the total cost of ownership exceeded $1,900. For a significant segment of the market, iOS was appealing but the economics were prohibitive.

The iPod touch 2nd generation addressed this directly. At $229 for the entry model, with no contract, no monthly fee, and no carrier lock-in, the 2G delivered the core of the iPhone experience over WiFi: the same App Store, the same Safari, the same Maps, Mail, YouTube, Calendar, and Music. The only things missing were cellular data, a phone, and GPS.

Apple announced 20 million cumulative iPod touch sales by February 2009, less than five months after the 2G launched. The device found its largest audiences among students, teenagers, international users in countries where the iPhone had not yet launched, and cost-conscious consumers who wanted iOS without committing to a carrier.

The revised 8GB model at $199 in September 2009 pushed this further. The iPod touch became the volume driver that expanded the iOS installed base beyond what the iPhone alone could have achieved — validating Apple’s belief that there was a market for a non-phone iOS device at a consumer price point.

The iPod touch 1st generation had a flat aluminum back, sharp edges, and a recessed headphone jack. The 2nd generation replaced all of it: a curved, polished stainless steel back that tapered toward the edges, matching the iPhone 3G's silhouette. Volume buttons appeared on the left edge. The speaker sat behind a grille at the top. The headphone jack sat flush.

This design became the template. The 3rd generation, announced in September 2009, was externally identical: same curved back, same dimensions, same button placement, same speaker position. The only way to distinguish a 2G from a 3G was to check the model number.

The 4th generation in September 2010 added a Retina display, cameras, and the A4 chip but retained the fundamental design language: curved stainless back, chrome edge, front-face proportions. The 2G's form factor defined what the iPod touch looked like for four consecutive hardware generations spanning 2008 through 2012.

It was not until the 5th generation in October 2012 that Apple broke the pattern entirely, introducing a thinner aluminum unibody with a 4-inch display. The stainless-and-chrome design language that the 2G had introduced was retired after four years.

data.heading:
Three major versions. Two eras.
One hardware ceiling.
data.title: Software lifecycle: iPhone OS 2.1.1 through iOS 4.2.1
paragraphs: The iPod touch 2nd generation shipped with iPhone OS 2.1.1 in September 2008 and received its final update, iOS 4.2.1, in November 2010 — a support window of just over two years across ten distinct OS versions.

When iOS 4.0 arrived in June 2010, it was the first major upgrade delivered free to iPod touch users. But the 2G received the new interface without three of iOS 4’s headline features: multitasking, custom home screen wallpapers, and Bluetooth keyboard support. The hardware’s memory and processor architecture simply could not sustain them.

When iOS 4.3 shipped in March 2011, the iPod touch 2nd generation was absent from the compatibility list entirely — not partially supported, simply gone. The App Store ecosystem began to move away within months.

body.subtitle: Paid software upgrades
body.text: iPod touch users were charged $9.95 for the iPhone OS 2.0 update (App Store access) and $9.95 again for iPhone OS 3.0, while iPhone users received both for free. Apple attributed the fee to Sarbanes-Oxley accounting regulations. The explanation was legally defensible but commercially unpopular — particularly given that the 3.0 update unlocked Bluetooth hardware that had been physically present in their device since purchase.

body.subtitle: Dormant Bluetooth chip
body.text: The 2nd generation shipped with a Samsung/Broadcom Bluetooth chip inside every unit from September 2008 onward, but the chip was disabled at the firmware level. It was not enabled until iPhone OS 3.0 in June 2009 — nine months after launch. Apple never publicly explained why the chip shipped dormant. The decision to charge $9.95 to unlock hardware the user already owned compounded the controversy.

body.subtitle: iOS 4 feature exclusions
body.text: When iOS 4.0 was released in June 2010, the 2G received the update but was excluded from multitasking, custom home screen wallpapers, and Bluetooth keyboard support. Some users and developers disputed this, noting that jailbroken 2G units could run basic multitasking with acceptable performance, and that the wallpaper restriction in particular seemed more like a product decision than a hardware limitation.

body.subtitle: Jailbreak and BootROM exploit
body.text: The original "MB" series models contained a hardware-level BootROM vulnerability that allowed unconditional jailbreaking — a persistent exploit that could not be patched via software update. Apple's response was the revised "MC" model in September 2009 with a patched BootROM. The original MB units remained permanently exploitable, creating a secondary market where un-patched 2G units commanded a premium.

body.subtitle: Performance degradation on iOS 4
body.text: Users who upgraded to iOS 4.0 widely reported slower performance and reduced responsiveness compared to iPhone OS 3.1.3. Apple did not offer a way to downgrade once the update was installed, leaving users on a version of the operating system their hardware was not fully equipped to run smoothly. This pattern would recur across Apple's product line in later years and eventually result in regulatory scrutiny.

hero.title: iPod touch
hero.subtitle: (2nd generation)
hero.desc: The second iPod touch fixed the most glaring omission of the first: it arrived with a built-in speaker. Redesigned with a rounded stainless back that echoed the iPhone 3G, it also added Nike+ wireless support without an adapter, external volume buttons, and a flush headphone jack. The same 3.5-inch display. Faster internals. A shape refined enough to last as the template for the next several generations.

overview.heading: The first iPod touch that felt finished.
paragraphs: The original iPod touch launched in 2007 as a screen-first proposition — a pocket-sized multi-touch display for music, the web, and eventually apps. It was remarkable hardware for its moment, but it shipped with one obvious gap: no speaker. Listening required headphones, always. The second generation closed that gap, and in doing so made the device feel categorically more useful.

Announced on September 9, 2008 at Apple's "Let's Rock" music-focused media event, the second-generation touch debuted alongside updated iPod nano and iPod classic models. It shipped the same day at $229 (8 GB), $299 (16 GB), and $399 (32 GB). The price positioned it squarely as a premium music device — not a phone, but closer to the total iPhone experience than anything else Apple made.

The redesign was substantial. The flat aluminum back of the first generation gave way to a polished stainless steel curved back that matched the iPhone 3G's aesthetic. The device became 30% thinner — 8.5 mm at its thickest, tapering toward the edges — and lighter at 115 grams. External volume buttons appeared on the left edge for the first time, the headphone jack was recessed flush with the casing, and the internal speaker sat behind a small grille at the top of the back panel.

Nike+ wireless support arrived without any external adapter. Where the original required a small receiver plugged into the dock connector to communicate with Nike+ sensor-equipped shoes, the second generation handled it natively over a built-in wireless module. For runners already in the Nike+ ecosystem, this alone was a meaningful upgrade.

Internally, the device carried a Samsung-manufactured ARM processor running at 533 MHz — faster than its predecessor — paired with 128 MB of RAM. It launched running iPhone OS 2.1 with full App Store access, a category the original touch received only via a $9.95 paid software update in 2008. The second generation had it from day one.

Software support extended through iOS 4.2.1, released in November 2010 — a notably extended lifespan for a device discontinued in June of that year. After discontinuation, the third generation (September 2009) continued with the same external design, differing primarily in processor speed. The second generation's form factor was, in effect, the template that defined the iPod touch's look for four years.

data.heading: From game changer to end of line.

events.title: iPod touch 3G announced and available.
events.preview: 50% faster. 256 MB RAM. Gaming GPU. Philip Schiller pitches it against the DS and PSP.
events.body:
Apple's "It's Only Rock and Roll" event unveiled the 3rd generation iPod touch. Philip Schiller led the introduction, positioning the device explicitly as a gaming platform and benchmarking it against the Nintendo DS and PlayStation Portable. The App Store already carried over 21,000 game titles.

Unlike previous iPod touch generations, the 3G launched and shipped on the same day. The 32 GB ($299) and 64 GB ($399) models were available immediately. An 8 GB model at $199 was also listed — but used 2nd generation internals, not the new Cortex-A8 hardware.

events.title: The 8GB discrepancy.
events.preview: Apple lists an 8GB model. It is a 2nd generation device in everything but name.
events.body:
Simultaneously with the keynote, Apple updated the entry-level price point with an 8 GB iPod touch at $199. This model did not carry the new 3rd generation internals — no Cortex-A8, no 256 MB RAM, no Voice Control hardware. It was the 2nd generation MC revision sold alongside the new device.

Apple never explicitly labelled it as 2nd generation in this context. Resellers and media compounded the confusion by listing it as a 3rd generation model. The distinction remained a persistent source of misidentification in secondary markets for years.

events.title: iPhone OS 3.1.3 — the last of the old naming.
events.preview: Final update before Apple renames the platform iOS. Bug fixes and security patches.
events.body:
iPhone OS 3.1.3 was the last software release to carry the "iPhone OS" name. It addressed battery accuracy reporting bugs and security vulnerabilities. No new features were introduced for iPod touch users.

The following summer, Apple rebranded the platform as iOS at WWDC 2010 — a deliberate move to signal that the operating system was no longer iPhone-centric. The 3rd generation iPod touch would receive every major iOS release through version 5.

events.title: iOS 4 preview — 3G confirmed for full support.
events.preview: Multitasking and wallpapers confirmed for 3G. The 2G is explicitly cut off.
events.body:
At Apple's iOS 4 preview event, the company confirmed that the 3rd generation iPod touch would receive full iOS 4 support — including native multitasking and custom home screen wallpapers. The 2nd generation was explicitly excluded from both features due to hardware limitations.

This confirmation drew a clear line between the two generations. The 3G's doubled RAM and Cortex-A8 architecture gave it the headroom the 2G lacked. For owners who had bought a 3G specifically for its internals, the announcement validated the purchase.

events.title: iOS 4.0 — full support, no upgrade fee.
events.preview: App folders, multitasking, wallpapers. First iPod touch major update shipped free.
events.body:
iOS 4 launched with complete feature support on the 3rd generation iPod touch. App folders, unified Mail, home screen wallpapers, and multitasking hooks all present — no exclusions, unlike the 2G's stripped-down iOS 4 experience.

Critically, this was the first major iOS upgrade delivered free to iPod touch users. Previous major versions — iPhone OS 2.0 and 3.0 — had required a $9.95 purchase due to Sarbanes-Oxley accounting rules. Apple cited a change in revenue recognition methodology for dropping the fee.

events.title: iPod touch 3G discontinued.
events.preview: One year on sale. Replaced by the 4th generation with Retina display and cameras.
events.body:
Apple discontinued the 3rd generation iPod touch on September 1, 2010 — exactly one year after launch — replacing it with the 4th generation iPod touch. The 4G brought Apple's A4 chip, a Retina display at 960×640, and both front and rear-facing cameras.

The camera inclusion on the 4G made the 3G's missing-camera story feel retroactively stranger. Whatever had prevented a camera in September 2009 had been resolved by September 2010. Apple never commented on the gap.

events.title: iOS 4.1 — Game Center arrives.
events.preview: Game Center launches on the 3G. Multiplayer matchmaking, leaderboards, achievements.
events.body:
iOS 4.1 introduced Game Center to the 3rd generation iPod touch — Apple's native multiplayer gaming platform with matchmaking, leaderboards, and achievements. The 3G's 256 MB RAM and SGX535 GPU made it a capable Game Center device for most titles through 2011.

The update also introduced HDR photo capabilities on devices with cameras — the 3G had no camera, but received the rest of the iOS 4.1 feature set without issue.

events.title: iOS 4.2.1 — AirPlay and Find My iPod.
events.preview: AirPlay, AirPrint, and free Find My iPod tracking come to the 3G.
events.body:
iOS 4.2.1 brought AirPlay audio and video streaming, AirPrint wireless printing, and a free tier of Find My iPod touch — previously a paid MobileMe feature — to the 3rd generation. The update unified the iOS feature set across iPhone, iPod touch, and iPad for the first time.

This was the same version number that ended 2nd generation software support entirely. For 3G owners, it was simply another update in a continuing sequence that would run for nearly two more years.

events.title: iOS 4.3 — Nitro JavaScript engine.
events.preview: Safari gets dramatically faster. Nitro engine transforms web browsing on the Cortex-A8.
events.body:
iOS 4.3 integrated the Nitro JavaScript engine into mobile Safari, delivering a dramatic improvement in web performance on the 3rd generation's Cortex-A8 processor. Benchmark scores roughly doubled. Pages that had felt sluggish loaded noticeably faster.

The update also brought iTunes Home Sharing improvements and Personal Hotspot — the latter iPhone-only, but the performance lift in Safari was universally felt. iOS 4.3 was the last significant feature update before iOS 5 completed the 3G's software lifecycle.

events.title: iOS 5.0 — iCloud, iMessage, Notification Center.
events.preview: The 3G's penultimate major version. OTA updates arrive. Siri does not.
events.body:
iOS 5 brought iCloud backup, iMessage Wi-Fi messaging, Notification Center, Reminders, and over-the-air updates to the 3rd generation iPod touch. It was the device's penultimate major iOS version and the first update that could be applied without connecting to a computer.

Siri, introduced simultaneously on iPhone 4S, was not available on the 3G. The 256 MB RAM ceiling became increasingly visible under iOS 5 — Safari tabs reloaded more aggressively, and the system carried a heavier memory footprint than iOS 4. The device remained functional but was beginning to show its age.

events.title: iOS 5.0.1 — first OTA bug fix.
events.preview: Battery life issues patched. The first purely over-the-air update Apple ever pushed.
events.body:
iOS 5.0.1 addressed significant battery drain issues that had emerged after the iOS 5.0 launch, along with bug fixes for iCloud storage syncing and accessibility improvements. It was delivered entirely over the air — no iTunes connection required — marking a milestone in how Apple distributed software updates.

For 3G users, the battery fix was particularly relevant given the device's already reduced audio playback time compared to the 2G.

events.title: iOS 5.1.1 — the final update.
events.preview: Bug fixes. End of the line. iOS 6 will not follow.
events.body:
iOS 5.1.1 was the last software update Apple delivered to the 3rd generation iPod touch. Released primarily as a stability and security fix — addressing iCloud syncing bugs, battery drainage, and Safari reliability — it closed the device's software lifecycle at 32 months from launch.

iOS 6, announced in June 2012 and released in September, excluded the device entirely. The iPhone 3GS — sharing the same ARMv7 Cortex-A8 architecture — received iOS 6. No explanation was offered for the asymmetric treatment.

events.title: iOS 6 drops the 3G.
events.preview: Same SoC family as iPhone 3GS, which got iOS 6. Apple said nothing.
events.body:
iOS 6 launched alongside the iPhone 5 and 5th generation iPod touch, with no support for the 3rd generation. The device's ARMv7 Cortex-A8 architecture nominally met the hardware requirements Apple cited for iOS 6 — the same SoC family used in the iPhone 3GS, which did receive iOS 6.

The practical consequence: a device discontinued in September 2010 lost active software support in September 2012. Less than 24 months of post-sale support for a device sold new at $299.

events.title: iOS 5.1.1 (9B206) — the goto fail patch.
events.preview: Apple patches a critical SSL vulnerability in a surprise legacy update. The absolute final code delivery to this hardware.
events.body:
In an unexpected move, Apple pushed a revised build of iOS 5.1.1 — build 9B206 — specifically to patch a severe SSL/TLS certificate verification vulnerability known as "goto fail." The bug allowed man-in-the-middle attacks against secure connections on affected devices.

This was the absolute final software modification Apple ever delivered to 3rd generation iPod touch hardware. No subsequent updates of any kind were issued. The device's software history ends here — a security patch, not a feature, as the last chapter.

What changed.
2nd → 3rd generation.
data.intro: The exterior did not change by a single millimetre. The interior changed almost completely. Apple ported the iPhone 3GS's processor platform into the iPod touch chassis — delivering the first iPod touch capable of console-quality mobile gaming.

data.heading: Two SKUs. No entry tier.
intro: The iPod touch 3rd generation was sold in two storage configurations only — 32 GB and 64 GB. The 8 GB tier was dropped entirely, and the 16 GB tier was never offered. This was the first iPod touch to ship without a sub-$300 option.

The 64 GB model was the highest-capacity iPod touch Apple had ever shipped at the time, and would remain so until the 4th generation. Both models launched September 9, 2009 and were discontinued simultaneously on September 1, 2010 — a lifespan of exactly one year.

body.text: No previous iPod touch had been sold primarily as a gaming device. The third generation changed that. Apple's September 2009 event benchmarked the 3G against the Nintendo DS and the Sony PlayStation Portable — two devices that had defined portable gaming for nearly a decade — and claimed superiority on available software alone. The App Store already carried over 21,000 game titles.

The hardware justified the pitch. The PowerVR SGX535 GPU supported OpenGL ES 2.0, enabling per-pixel lighting, bloom effects, and shader-driven rendering that the previous generation's MBX Lite could not produce. Titles like Modern Combat, Infinity Blade, and Real Racing were built specifically for the 3G's graphics ceiling.

Doubled RAM changed the experience more subtly but more fundamentally. The 2nd generation's 128 MB ceiling forced developers to aggressively compress assets and limit scene complexity. At 256 MB, the 3G could hold larger textures, run more complex physics, and switch between apps without the hard reloads that characterized its predecessor.

The 3G's commercial timing was fortunate. iOS gaming was entering its first serious growth phase, and the 3G arrived exactly as the market needed a non-phone device capable of running its most demanding titles. It seeded a generation of players who had no console — only a pocket-sized slab with a touch screen and an App Store account.

The 3rd generation iPod touch was externally indistinguishable from the 2nd generation. Same curved polished stainless steel back. Same flush 3.5 mm headphone jack. Same 110 × 61.8 × 8.5 mm footprint. Same weight. The home button, the dock connector, the volume buttons — unchanged. A user holding both devices simultaneously could not tell them apart by touch.

This was a deliberate choice. Apple had invested in the 2G chassis — the curved stainless rear, the form that sat better in the hand than the flat aluminum of the original — and saw no reason to retire it after a single cycle. The industrial design story for the 3G was not the shell but the interior: what Apple had managed to fit inside an unchanged body.

The one visible difference was in the retail box. The 3G shipped with the new earbuds including a three-button remote and microphone — the same accessory included with the iPhone 3GS. The EarPods era was still two years away, but these earbuds represented a meaningful upgrade over the plain earbuds in previous iPod touch boxes.

For case manufacturers, the unchanged design was a gift and, briefly, a source of embarrassment. Cases designed for the 2G fit the 3G perfectly — but those same manufacturers had already tooled up for a 3G with a rear camera cutout, based on leaked designs that never materialised. For a few weeks in September 2009, camera cases for a camera-less device sat on the shelves at Best Buy.

data.heading:
Three major versions. Nearly three years.
One cliff.
data.title: Software lifecycle: iPhone OS 3.1.1 through iOS 5.1.1
paragraphs: The iPod touch 3rd generation launched on iPhone OS 3.1.1 and received full software support for nearly three years — a notably longer run than the 2nd generation's two-year window. The Cortex-A8 architecture gave it headroom the ARM11-based 2G lacked, enabling it to run iOS 4 without the feature exclusions that hobbled its predecessor.

Unlike the 2G, which received iOS 4 in a crippled form — no multitasking, no wallpapers, no Bluetooth keyboard — the 3G received iOS 4 fully. Multitasking, Game Center, FaceTime prep, AirPlay: all present. The 3G was the minimum viable platform for iOS 4's marquee features.

The end came with iOS 6 in September 2012. The 3G's ARMv7 architecture technically met iOS 6's baseline requirements, making the cutoff a product decision rather than a hardware necessity. Apple's stated reason was optimisation; the practical effect was that a device sold until September 2010 lost software support less than two years after discontinuation.

notes.label: iOS 4.0
notes.text: Full iOS 4 support — multitasking, wallpapers, Game Center. No feature exclusions unlike 2nd gen.

notes.label: iOS 5.1.1
notes.text: Final official update. May 7, 2012. ARMv7 architecture met iOS 6 requirements; Apple still cut it.

notes.label: iOS 6
notes.text: Device dropped from compatibility list. ARMv7 requirement met but Apple chose not to support.

body.subtitle: The missing camera
body.text: Before the September 9 launch, leaked images showed a 3rd generation iPod touch prototype with a rear camera centerd on the back panel. Case manufacturers — including products stocked at Best Buy retail locations — built and shipped camera-cutout cases based on these leaks. When the device launched with no camera and an unchanged back panel, the disconnect was immediate. A subsequent iFixit teardown of the 3rd generation confirmed the story: the camera socket was physically present inside the device. The hardware had been designed to accommodate a camera. Something — widely attributed to manufacturing yield problems with the camera module — removed it from the final product. Apple never commented. Prototypes with functioning cameras later surfaced on eBay in 2010, corroborating the teardown findings.

body.subtitle: The 8GB labeling confusion
body.text: At launch, Apple continued selling the 2nd generation iPod touch in 8 GB form alongside the new 3G. Resellers — not Apple — began labeling these as "3rd generation," creating persistent confusion in secondary markets that lasted years. The 8 GB model was hardware-identical to the original 2nd gen MC revision: same ARM11 processor, same 128 MB RAM, same GPU. It was not a 3rd generation device by any internal measure. Apple never publicly addressed the mislabeling.

body.subtitle: The iOS 6 cutoff
body.text: The 3G's ARMv7 Cortex-A8 architecture nominally met the hardware requirements Apple later cited for iOS 6 compatibility. The decision to exclude it was not driven by an absolute hardware barrier — the iPhone 3GS, using the same SoC family, received iOS 6. The practical effect was that owners of a device discontinued in September 2010 lost software support in September 2012: a window of less than 24 months post-sale.

hero.title: iPod touch
hero.subtitle: (3rd generation)
hero.desc: The third iPod touch wore the same face as the second but hid a fundamentally different machine inside. A new processor, doubled RAM, and a gaming-grade GPU transformed it from a music player that could run apps into something Apple had never explicitly made before: a dedicated handheld gaming device.

overview.heading: The fastest iPod touch ever made.
paragraphs: The third-generation iPod touch was announced September 9, 2009 at Apple's "It's Only Rock and Roll" music event — the same event that introduced iTunes 9 and refreshed the iPod lineup. In a break from the iPhone-centric framing of previous iPod touch launches, Apple positioned the 3G almost entirely around gaming, benchmarking it against the Nintendo DS and PlayStation Portable.

Inside the unchanged aluminum and stainless steel chassis sat hardware borrowed directly from the iPhone 3GS: a Samsung ARMv7 Cortex-A8 core clocked at 600 MHz, the PowerVR SGX535 GPU with OpenGL ES 2.0 support, and 256 MB of RAM — double the 2nd generation's ceiling. Apple called it "50% faster." In practice the gap was wider, particularly in 3D games where the SGX535's shader pipeline ran circles around the older MBX Lite.

The storage lineup contracted sharply. Gone was the 8 GB entry tier and the 16 GB mid-tier. The 3rd generation shipped in 32 GB and 64 GB only — the latter the largest iPod touch Apple had ever shipped. Pricing held at $299 and $399.
One notable first: the 3rd generation was the first iPod touch to ship with earbuds that included a remote and microphone, enabling Voice Control — a feature previously exclusive to iPhone 3GS.

What Apple did not announce was a camera. Pre-release leaks, third-party case packaging at Best Buy, and a subsequent iFixit teardown all told the same story: the 3rd generation was designed to include a rear camera, the socket was physically present inside the device, and something — a manufacturing problem, a cost decision, or a strategic choice — removed it at the last moment. Apple said nothing.

iOS support extended to iOS 5.1.1, released May 2012 — nearly three years of updates. The device could not run iOS 6, which required ARMv7 features the 3G's SoC technically met but Apple chose not to support.

photos.caption: The 3.5-inch Retina display — 326 ppi, the headline feature of the 4th generation.
At 7.2 mm and 86 g, the thinnest and lightest iPod touch to that point.
The aluminum back with the protruding rear camera — the first camera in the line.

data.heading: Three years. One screen that changed everything.

events.title: iPod touch 4G announced.
events.preview: Retina display. Cameras. FaceTime. 26% thinner. The iPhone 4's sibling without the phone.
events.body:
Apple announced the 4th generation iPod touch at its annual music event on September 1, 2010. Phil Schiller led the presentation, positioning it as the device that brought the iPhone 4's most significant features — the Retina display, FaceTime, dual cameras — to the iPod touch line without requiring a carrier contract.

The Retina display at 326 PPI was the headline. The cameras — front-facing FaceTime, rear-facing 720p video — were the second headline. The device was 26% thinner than the 3rd generation and 25% lighter. It launched September 12 in black at $229 (8 GB), $299 (32 GB), and $399 (64 GB).

events.title: iPod touch 4G goes on sale.
events.preview: Available in stores. Black only. 8, 32, 64 GB. iOS 4.1 out of the box.
events.body:
The 4th generation iPod touch went on sale September 12, 2010, shipping with iOS 4.1. The release coincided with the public launch of Game Center — Apple's multiplayer gaming platform — which arrived in the same iOS update.

An iFixit teardown the same week confirmed the device's 256 MB of RAM — half the 512 MB in the iPhone 4, and equal to the iPad. The finding drew immediate attention from developers and enthusiasts who noted the RAM gap would have long-term implications for software support.

events.title: 8 GB price drops to $199.
events.preview: Entry-tier now $199. Mass-market positioning solidified.
events.body: Apple reduced the price of the 8 GB iPod touch from $229 to $199 in October 2010, establishing it as a direct competitor to entry-level portable gaming devices. The price cut positioned the iPod touch explicitly against the Nintendo DS ($149–$179) and Sony PSP ($169–$199) — devices Apple had been benchmarking against since the 3rd generation launch.

events.title: White model announced.
events.preview: A second color — over a year after launch. Announced alongside iPhone 4S.
events.body: Apple announced the white iPod touch 4th generation at its "Let's Talk iPhone" event on October 4, 2011 — the same event that introduced the iPhone 4S and, notably, was Steve Jobs's last Apple product event before his death the following day. The white model went on sale October 12, 2011 alongside iOS 5.0.

events.title: iOS 5.0 — iCloud, iMessage, OTA updates.
events.preview: The 4G gets iCloud, iMessage, Newsstand, and the first OTA software update.
events.body: iOS 5 brought iCloud backup, iMessage Wi-Fi messaging, Notification Center, Reminders, and over-the-air updates to the 4th generation iPod touch. It was the first iOS update that required no computer connection. The 4G's 256 MB RAM showed its limitations under iOS 5 — Safari tabs reloaded more aggressively — but the core experience remained functional.

events.title: 5th gen launches. 4G lineup restructured.
events.preview: 8 and 64 GB discontinued. 16 GB added at $199. 32 GB drops to $249.
events.body:
Apple announced the 5th generation iPod touch on September 12, 2012 — the same day as the iPhone 5. Simultaneously, the 4th generation lineup was restructured: the 8 GB and 64 GB models were discontinued, a new 16 GB model was introduced at $199, and the 32 GB price dropped to $249.

The 4th generation continued as the budget option in Apple's iPod touch lineup, sitting below the new 5th generation's $229 starting price. Both continued to be sold in parallel.

events.title: iPod touch 4G discontinued.
events.preview: Eleven days before iOS 7 is announced. Apple says nothing about the timing.
events.body:
Apple discontinued the final 4th generation iPod touch models — the 16 GB and 32 GB — on May 29, 2013. The device had been on sale for nearly three years, across four storage tiers and two colors.

What Apple did not announce was that iOS 7 — which would explicitly exclude the 4th generation — would be revealed eleven days later at WWDC 2013. Customers who purchased new 4th generation hardware in the final days of its sale had no way to know they were buying a device that would be left behind by the current iOS within weeks.

events.title: iOS 7 announced — 4G not supported.
events.preview: WWDC 2013. iOS 7 requires 512 MB RAM. The 4G has 256 MB. It is excluded.
events.body:
iOS 7 was announced at WWDC on June 10, 2013 — eleven days after the 4th generation was discontinued. The compatibility list did not include the iPod touch 4th generation. Apple's stated reasoning centerd on RAM requirements: iOS 7 needed more memory than the 4G's 256 MB could provide.

The iPhone 4 — with the same A4 processor family but 512 MB of RAM — received iOS 7. The asymmetric treatment highlighted the deliberate RAM difference Apple had built into the 2010 A4 device lineup, a decision that had seemed like a cost measure at the time but functioned as a structural end-of-life mechanism.

events.title: iOS 6.1.5 — FaceTime fix.
events.preview: Surprise update. FaceTime calls had been failing. Apple patches the discontinued device.
events.body: Apple issued iOS 6.1.5 for the iPod touch 4th generation on November 14, 2013, six months after the device's discontinuation. The update addressed a bug causing FaceTime calls to fail — a particularly relevant fix for a device whose FaceTime capability had been a primary selling point.

events.title: iOS 6.1.6 — goto fail. The final update.
events.preview: Critical SSL patch. The last code Apple ever delivered to this hardware.
events.body:
iOS 6.1.6 was released February 21, 2014 — the same goto fail SSL security patch issued simultaneously for the iPhone 3GS. It addressed a severe certificate verification vulnerability that had been discovered in Apple's TLS implementation.

This was the absolute final software update Apple delivered to the 4th generation iPod touch. The device's software history ends here: a security patch, not a feature, as the last act. The hardware had been discontinued nine months prior. The final update arrived nearly 3.5 years after launch.

data.heading:
What changed.
3rd → 4th generation.
data.intro: The third generation changed nothing on the outside. The fourth generation changed almost everything — the display, the cameras, the thickness, the weight. For the first time, the iPod touch looked and felt like a genuinely new product rather than an internal upgrade.

data.heading: Three years. Four tiers. Two phases.
intro: The iPod touch 4th generation had the most complex SKU history of any iPod touch to that point. It launched in three capacities in September 2010, received a price reduction on the entry tier in October 2010, added a white color option in October 2011, added a 16 GB mid-tier in September 2012, and discontinued the 8 GB and 64 GB in the same month.
The 16 and 32 GB models continued until May 29, 2013 — the longest any 4th gen SKU stayed on sale, at nearly three years. The final lineup before discontinuation was 16 GB at $199 and 32 GB at $249.
data.footer: All configurations: 800 MHz Apple A4 · 256 MB RAM · 3.5″ Retina 960×640 · 326 ppi · 0.7 MP + 0.3 MP cameras · 7.2 mm · 86.3 g

body.text: When Apple introduced FaceTime with the iPhone 4 in June 2010, it required a phone. Specifically, an iPhone 4, on AT&T, in the United States, calling another iPhone 4. The feature was genuinely remarkable — and practically limited to a narrow audience.

The 4th generation iPod touch changed the audience. FaceTime over Wi-Fi, on a device with no carrier requirement, no monthly bill, and a price starting at $229, brought video calling to students, to children, to anyone with a Wi-Fi connection. The iPod touch became the first mass-market video communication device that wasn't a laptop.

For families separated by geography, for students away at school, for children too young for a smartphone, the 4G iPod touch became the de facto FaceTime terminal for the first few years of video calling's mainstream adoption. Apple TV commercials throughout 2010 and 2011 — some of the most emotionally direct advertising Apple ever made — showed FaceTime conversations between grandparents and grandchildren, between soldiers and families. Nearly all of those ads used the iPod touch.

The gyroscope added another dimension to gaming that the 3G's accelerometer-only setup had lacked. Combined with the Retina display's pixel density — which made games look definitively better than any competing portable device — the 4G became the platform of choice for the most graphically ambitious App Store titles of 2011 and 2012. Infinity Blade, Real Racing 2, and Dead Space were designed around its capabilities.

photos.caption: Video calling over Wi-Fi, no carrier contract required — the 4th gen brought it to the masses.

data.heading: Thinner than the phone it resembled.

body.text: The fourth generation iPod touch was 7.2 mm thin — 15% thinner than the 3rd generation's 8.5 mm, and actually slimmer than the iPhone 4 it visually referenced. At 86.3 grams, it weighed 25% less than its predecessor. Apple achieved this by moving away from the stainless steel-backed design of the 2nd and 3rd generations toward a polished aluminum rear with chamfered edges.

The front face was entirely new: a Retina display with oleophobic coating, the same fingerprint-resistant treatment used on the iPhone 4. The volume buttons moved to the left edge. The headphone jack remained flush on the bottom — one of the iPod touch's distinguishing design elements since the second generation.

The device initially launched in black only. The white model followed in October 2011, announced at the same event as the iPhone 4S. White iPod touch models had been rare — the original iPod touch came in silver, and no white was offered until the 4th generation. Apple offered the 4G in both colors through the end of its sales lifecycle.

The slimming came with a cost that went unannounced: the rear camera protrudes from the back panel, creating a slight bump. On a device this thin, the camera module's depth was difficult to conceal. Apple chose performance over flush aesthetics — a tradeoff that would appear on every iPhone from the 6 onward and become an accepted convention of modern smartphone design.

photos.caption: The polished aluminum back and chamfered edges — 15% thinner than the 3rd generation.
Introduced October 2011, over a year after the black launch — the first white iPod touch.

data.heading: Three major versions. One sharp cliff.
data.title: Software lifecycle: iOS 4.1 through iOS 6.1.6
paragraphs: The 4th generation iPod touch launched on iOS 4.1 and received full support through iOS 5.1.1, and partial support in iOS 6 — three major iOS versions total, the longest software run of any iPod touch up to that point. It received every feature its hardware could support: iCloud, iMessage, Game Center, Siri (dictation only, not the full assistant), Maps, FaceTime improvements.

The iOS 7 exclusion was the defining controversy of the device's lifecycle. The 4G shared its Apple A4 processor architecture with the iPhone 4 — which received iOS 7. The difference was RAM: 256 MB on the iPod touch, 512 MB on the iPhone 4. Apple determined that iOS 7 was not viable on 256 MB, a judgment validated by independent testing showing the iPhone 4 itself ran iOS 7 poorly.

The timing was the problem. The 16 GB iPod touch 4th generation was sold as new hardware — at $199 — until May 29, 2013. Apple announced iOS 7 at WWDC on June 10, 2013: eleven days later. A customer who bought the device the day before discontinuation could not run the current iOS within two weeks of purchase. Apple offered no acknowledgment of the timing, no transition assistance, and no official comment.

notes.label: iOS 6.0
notes.text: Partial iOS 6 support — Maps, Passbook, Siri dictation (not full assistant). Last major version.

notes.label: iOS 7
notes.text: Excluded — 256 MB RAM vs required 512 MB. iPhone 4 with same A4 SoC received iOS 7.

notes.label: iOS 6.1.6
notes.text: Post-EOL security patch — the goto fail SSL fix, Feb 21 2014. Final Apple software delivery to this hardware.

body.subtitle: The 0.7 megapixel rear camera
body.text: The 4th generation iPod touch launched with a rear camera capable of 720p video — but still images were captured at 0.7 megapixels. The iPhone 4, announced three months earlier and sharing the same A4 processor family, had a 5-megapixel rear camera. Apple's decision to fit a substantially inferior still camera into the iPod touch was widely criticized. The gap was not subtle: the iPhone 4's camera was seven times higher resolution. Reviewers at the time speculated that Apple deliberately limited the iPod touch camera to protect iPhone margins and maintain a clear product hierarchy. Apple did not comment on the specification decision.

body.subtitle: The iOS 7 timing problem
body.text: Apple discontinued the final 16 GB and 32 GB models of the 4th generation iPod touch on May 29, 2013. WWDC — where Apple announced iOS 7 — began eleven days later, on June 10. A customer who purchased the device new on May 28, 2013 would find, within two weeks, that the current iOS was incompatible with their new purchase. Apple offered no warning in the retail channel, no acknowledgment after the announcement, and no transition path. The company's position that iOS 7 required more RAM than the device carried was technically defensible — the iPhone 4, with 512 MB, already ran iOS 7 poorly — but the timing made it indefensible to customers.

body.subtitle: 256 MB RAM — a ceiling the iPhone 4 didn't have
body.text: All three A4-based devices released in 2010 — the iPad, the iPod touch 4th generation, and the iPhone 4 — used the same Apple A4 processor. Apple gave the iPhone 4 512 MB of RAM. It gave the iPad and iPod touch 256 MB. The RAM differential had no immediate consequence in 2010, when iOS 4 ran adequately on 256 MB. Over time, as iOS updates consumed more memory, the gap widened. Safari tabs reloaded more aggressively, multitasking was more constrained, and the ultimate consequence was iOS 7 exclusion — an exclusion the iPhone 4, with its doubled RAM, avoided. The RAM decision looked like a cost-saving measure at launch; it looked like planned obsolescence by 2013.

photos.caption: 720p video but only 0.7 MP stills — a fraction of the iPhone 4’s 5 MP sensor.
The protruding rear camera module — widely criticized for image quality at launch.
Enthusiasts later ported iOS 7 to the 4th gen — the version Apple said its 256 MB RAM couldn’t run.

hero.title: iPod touch
hero.subtitle: (4th generation)
hero.desc: The fourth generation iPod touch was the device that finally made people believe the iPod touch mattered. A Retina display sharp enough to embarrass every screen around it. Cameras — both front and rear — for the first time in the line's history. FaceTime without a phone plan. It was the iPhone 4's closest cousin, and for millions of people who couldn't afford or didn't want a carrier contract, it was the better deal.

overview.heading: The iPhone 4, without the phone.
paragraphs: The fourth-generation iPod touch was announced September 1, 2010 at Apple's annual iPod event and released twelve days later. It arrived in the same season as the iPhone 4, and Apple made no secret of the relationship — the two devices shared the same Apple A4 processor, the same Retina display at 960×640 and 326 PPI, the same FaceTime capability, and a form factor that was, at 7.2 mm, actually thinner than the iPhone 4.

The headline features were the cameras. For the first time in the iPod touch's history, the device had both a front-facing FaceTime camera and a rear-facing iSight camera capable of 720p video. FaceTime over Wi-Fi — Apple's video calling system, introduced months earlier with the iPhone 4 — was now available to anyone, without a phone plan or a carrier contract. For schools, for children, for anyone who wanted a connected device without a monthly bill, this was the entry point.

The Retina display was the other watershed moment. The jump from the 3G's 163 PPI to 326 PPI was not incremental — it was a step change visible to the naked eye from the first glance. Text sharpened. Photos clarified. Games rendered at a pixel density that, in 2010, had no competition.

The hardware story had complications. The A4 chip ran at 800 MHz, faster than the 3G's 600 MHz, but the RAM stayed at 256 MB — half the 512 MB Apple put in the iPhone 4. The rear camera, despite producing 720p video, captured stills at only 0.7 megapixels — a figure that drew immediate criticism given the iPhone 4's 5 MP camera sat in the same device family.

The 4th generation had the longest sales lifespan of any iPod touch to that point: nearly three years, across multiple price drops and a mid-cycle expansion of the SKU lineup. It was discontinued in two phases — the 8 and 64 GB models in October 2012, the 16 and 32 GB models in May 2013 — and its final software update, iOS 6.1.6, arrived in February 2014.

data.heading: Six colors. Three years. One budget controversy.

events.title: iPod touch 5G announced.
events.preview: 4-inch Retina. 5 MP camera. Siri. Six colors. Lightning. Same day as the iPhone 5.
events.body:
Apple announced the 5th generation iPod touch at its iPhone 5 event on September 12, 2012. The announcement covered every major upgrade: the larger 4-inch 1136×640 Retina display in 16:9 widescreen, the dual-core Apple A5 processor with 512 MB RAM, the 5 MP iSight camera with LED flash and 1080p video, and Siri — all for the first time on an iPod touch.

The color range — Slate, Silver, Pink, Yellow, Blue — was announced at the same event, each with a matching wrist loop. The Lightning connector replaced the 30-pin dock. Release date was set for October 11, 2012.

events.title: iPod touch 5G goes on sale.
events.preview: 32 GB and 64 GB, five colors, iOS 6. The loop is included in the box.
events.body:
The 5th generation iPod touch went on sale October 11, 2012, shipping with iOS 6. Launch configurations were 32 GB at $299 and 64 GB at $399, in Slate, Silver, Pink, Yellow, and Blue. The iPod touch Loop — a color-matched wrist strap that attached via a pop-out button on the back — was included.

The 16 GB tier was absent. Apple would not offer a 16 GB 5G until May 2013, and that model would arrive without the rear camera.

events.title: PRODUCT(RED) variant released.
events.preview: A sixth color joins the lineup. Red with white front. Proceeds support the Global Fund.
events.body: Apple released the PRODUCT(RED) iPod touch 5th generation in November 2012, completing the color lineup. Like all non-Slate models, the RED variant has a white front. A portion of proceeds from PRODUCT(RED) purchases go to the Global Fund to fight AIDS, tuberculosis, and malaria.

events.title: 16 GB A1509 quietly added — no rear camera.
events.preview: An entry-level 5G with no iSight camera, no loop, Silver only. No press release.
events.body:
Apple silently added a 16 GB iPod touch 5th generation (model A1509) at $229 — the same price point previously occupied by the 4th generation. This model omits the rear iSight camera, the LED flash, and the loop attachment button. It comes only in a Silver finish with a black front and is not sold with a loop.

The addition received no press release. It drew immediate critical attention, with reviewers noting that consumers buying a 5th generation iPod touch at $229 might not realise they were getting a device without the camera that defined the 5G's launch.

events.title: Space Gray replaces Slate.
events.preview: The darkest color is renamed alongside the iPhone 5s and 5c launch.
events.body: Apple renamed the Slate color option to Space Gray on September 10, 2013, alongside the announcement of the iPhone 5s and iPhone 5c. The color itself — a dark anodised aluminum — remained essentially unchanged; the renaming aligned the iPod touch's color nomenclature with the broader Apple product line.

events.title: A1421 16 GB with camera. A1509 discontinued. Price drops.
events.preview: The camera returns to the entry tier. All six colors. Prices fall across the board.
events.body:
Apple overhauled the 5G lineup on June 26, 2014. The A1509 was discontinued. A proper 16 GB A1421 — with the 5 MP iSight camera, LED flash, loop button, and all six colors — was introduced at $199. The 32 GB dropped from $299 to $249. The 64 GB dropped from $399 to $299.

The move acknowledged, implicitly, that the A1509's camera omission had been a mistake. The 5G lineup was finally complete and consistent across all three capacities.

events.title: 5th generation discontinued.
events.preview: 6th generation announced. The 5G's three-year run ends.
events.body: Apple discontinued the 5th generation iPod touch on July 14, 2015 with the announcement of the 6th generation. The 6G kept the same chassis and screen, but moved to an Apple A8 processor — the chip from the iPhone 6 — and upgraded the rear camera to 8 megapixels. The Loop was removed. The color lineup was restructured.

events.title: iOS 9 — partial support.
events.preview: Full iOS 9 except Transit in Maps. The A5 held up well.
events.body: iOS 9 shipped in September 2015 and the 5th generation received it in full, with one exception: the Transit feature in Maps — which provided real-time public transport navigation — was not available on the 5G. All other iOS 9 features, including the split-screen and picture-in-picture capabilities (though the 5G's screen was too small for practical split-screen use), ran correctly.

events.title: iOS 9.3.5 — the final update.
events.preview: Critical security patch. The last code Apple ever shipped to this hardware.
events.body:
Apple released iOS 9.3.5 on August 25, 2016 — a security patch for a critical vulnerability in WebKit and the kernel, discovered by the Citizen Lab and used in targeted attacks. It was delivered to the 5th generation iPod touch, the iPhone 4S, and other 32-bit devices that had already been excluded from iOS 10.

This was the last software update Apple delivered to the 5th generation. iOS 10, released three weeks later on September 13, 2016, dropped all 32-bit devices. The 5G's software history ends here.

data.heading:
What changed.
4th → 5th generation.
data.intro: The fourth generation doubled down on cameras and display quality. The fifth generation doubled everything else — processor cores, RAM, camera resolution, Wi-Fi bands, Bluetooth version, and color options — while simultaneously moving to a new taller screen format and a new connector. It was the largest generational leap in the iPod touch's history.

data.heading: Six colors. Three tiers. One stripped-down exception.
intro: The 5th generation iPod touch launched in two capacities — 32 GB and 64 GB — in five colors. The 16 GB tier arrived later in two distinct phases: first as the A1509, a stripped-down model without a rear camera or loop button, then as the full-featured A1421 with all six colors restored.

All A1421 configurations share the same hardware. The A1509 was the sole exception: same chassis, same display, same processor, but without the rear camera, without the LED flash, and without the loop button — and sold only in Silver.

body.text: The fifth generation iPod touch did something no iPod touch had done before: it made you choose. Not just between capacities — between a color that expressed something about you. Slate, Silver, Pink, Yellow, Blue, and PRODUCT(RED) were not just finish options. Apple sold each one with a matching wrist loop in the same shade, making the device feel like an accessory as much as a computer.

This was deliberate. Apple's advertising in 2012 and 2013 leaned hard into the color story — campaign imagery of people holding colorful iPods against colorful backgrounds, loop straps worn visibly. The 5G was the first iPod touch to appear in television commercials that had nothing to do with its technical capabilities and everything to do with how it looked on your wrist.

The gaming dimension was equally significant. The A5's PowerVR SGX543MP2 GPU delivered roughly seven times the graphics performance of the A4 — and developers noticed immediately. Infinity Blade II (2011, ported to benefit from A5 iPad) became the showcase game for the 5G. Real Racing 3, Asphalt 8, and later XCOM: Enemy Unknown were all designed with the A5 in mind. By 2013, the App Store had crossed 900,000 apps, and the 5G was the primary gaming device for a generation of players who couldn't afford or didn't need a phone.

Siri on the iPod touch was quietly significant. Apple had kept its voice assistant iPhone-exclusive for a year, using it as a differentiator for the 4S. Bringing it to the 5G democratised the feature — and opened a device that could answer questions, set timers, and play music by voice to an audience that included children too young for a phone contract.

data.heading: Thinner than the phone it resembled. Lighter than you expected.

body.text: The fifth generation iPod touch was 6.1 mm thin — the thinnest iPod touch ever made, and thinner than the iPhone 5 (7.6 mm) it shared its design language with. Despite the larger screen, it was barely heavier than the 4th generation: 88 g versus 86 g. Apple achieved this with a lightweight aluminum rear that, unlike the polished finish of the 4th generation, was anodised in each of the six available colors.

The anodising process was central to the color story. Each device's aluminum back was chemically treated to produce a durable, integral color — not a coating that could chip or wear. The color went into the metal. This process, the same used for the iPhone 5, was more expensive than painting, and Apple had been refining it since the colored iPod nano. The result was a device that felt premium in every color, not just silver.

The 4-inch display maintained 326 PPI by moving from the 3:2 aspect ratio of all previous iPod touch screens to the 16:9 widescreen format of the iPhone 5. This meant 176 additional vertical pixels — enough for a fifth row of app icons on the home screen and letterbox-free playback of widescreen video. The extra height also accommodated a panorama mode camera, available for the first time on the iPod touch.

The pop-out loop button sat in the lower-left of the back. Pressing it ejected a small metal nub from the chassis, to which a color-matched wrist loop could be attached. The mechanism was simple, the execution elegant — and just fragile enough to generate its own forum thread when units began snapping. The loop was included with 32 GB and 64 GB models; 16 GB models could purchase it separately.

data.heading: Three full versions. One partial. Then the 32-bit cliff.
data.title: Software lifecycle: iOS 6.0 through iOS 9.3.5
paragraphs: The 5th generation iPod touch launched with iOS 6 and received three full major versions — iOS 6, 7, and 8 — before hitting partial support in iOS 9. It was the first iPod touch to support Siri, Maps turn-by-turn navigation, and Panorama camera from day one. It received every major iOS feature through iOS 8 that its hardware could support: AirDrop, Touch ID activation (though it had no sensor, the framework was present), Continuity, and App Extensions.

iOS 9 (September 2015) was the first version where the 5G's support became meaningfully incomplete. The device ran iOS 9 but did not support the Transit feature in Maps — the real-time public transport navigation that required server-side infrastructure Apple had not built out for all devices. All other iOS 9 features ran correctly.

The iOS 10 exclusion was categorical. iOS 10 (September 2016) dropped all 32-bit devices — the iPhone 4S, iPad 2, iPad mini (1st gen), and the iPod touch 5th gen among them. Apple's stated reason was 64-bit architecture requirements. The A5 was a 32-bit processor and could not run iOS 10's 64-bit-required kernel. iOS 9.3.5, released August 25, 2016, was the final update — a security patch for a critical kernel vulnerability, delivered to the device after it had already been excluded from iOS 10.

notes.label: iOS 6–8
notes.text: Full support — Siri, Maps turn-by-turn, AirDrop, Continuity, App Extensions. All flagship features.

notes.label: iOS 9
notes.text: Partial — all features except Transit in Maps. Device ran iOS 9 well; A5's 512 MB held up.

notes.label: iOS 9.3.5
notes.text: Final update — security patch for critical kernel vulnerability. Aug 25, 2016.

notes.label: iOS 10
notes.text: Excluded — 32-bit A5 dropped system-wide. iPhone 4S, iPad mini (1st gen) fell simultaneously.

body.subtitle: The A1509: a 5th gen without the 5th gen's headline feature
body.text: In May 2013, Apple added a 16 GB iPod touch to the lineup at $229 — but this model (A1509) had no rear camera, no LED flash, no loop button, and came only in Silver. It was sold as a 5th generation iPod touch with no prominent indication that it lacked the camera that had been the centerpiece of the 5G's September 2012 launch. A customer buying an iPod touch 5th gen at $229 in 2013 might reasonably expect a 5 MP camera. They would not get one. Apple discontinued the A1509 in June 2014, quietly, when it restored the camera to the 16 GB tier at $199.

body.subtitle: Lightning broke everything
body.text: The iPod touch 5G was the first in the line to use Apple's new Lightning connector, replacing the 30-pin dock connector that had been the standard since 2003. Every dock speaker, car integration, alarm clock, and accessory built for the 30-pin iPod was instantly obsolete. Apple sold a 30-pin to Lightning adapter for $29 — a separate purchase required to use equipment the previous iPod touch had worked with natively. The transition was technically correct (Lightning was superior in every measurable way), but it landed on consumers as an expensive inconvenience.

body.subtitle: The A5 was already a year old on launch day
body.text: The iPhone 5, announced the same day, shipped with the Apple A6 — a new 32-bit dual-core processor with custom Apple-designed Swift cores, running at 1.3 GHz with significantly better single-thread performance than the A5. The 5G iPod touch launched with the A5, the same chip Apple had shipped in the iPhone 4S in October 2011 and in the iPad 2 in March 2011. By the time the 5G shipped, the A5 was over a year old. Apple's reasoning — cost management for a device at a lower price point — was defensible. But it meant the iPod touch launched behind the current iPhone on the day of its own announcement, a pattern that would continue in subsequent generations.

hero.subtitle: (5th generation)
hero.desc: The fifth generation iPod touch arrived in six colors, with a 5 MP camera, Siri, a 4-inch Retina display, and a playful pop-out wrist loop. It was faster, thinner, more capable, and more colorful than anything before it in the line — and it arrived the same day as the iPhone 5, sharing its design language without its price. For millions of people who wanted an iPhone but not a contract, the 5G was the answer.

overview.heading: The iPhone 5's closest relative — and the most colorful iPod ever made.
paragraphs: The fifth generation iPod touch was announced on September 12, 2012 alongside the iPhone 5 and went on sale October 11. It was a sweeping redesign: the display grew from 3.5 to 4 inches, the resolution moved to 1136×640 in a 16:9 aspect ratio, the rear camera jumped from 0.7 megapixels to 5 megapixels with an LED flash and 1080p video, and the processor moved from the single-core A4 to the dual-core A5 — doubling RAM from 256 MB to 512 MB in the process. The 30-pin dock connector was replaced with Lightning.

The headline, though, was color. Apple offered the 5th generation in Slate, Silver, Pink, Yellow, and Blue at launch — a range of options the iPod touch had never had. Each color came with a matching wrist loop, attached via a pop-out button on the lower-left of the back. A PRODUCT(RED) variant followed in November 2012, completing what became the most distinctive iPod touch lineup in the line's history.

Siri arrived on the iPod touch for the first time. Previously restricted to the iPhone 4S and later the iPad, Apple's voice assistant now worked on a device without a phone plan. Combined with the 5 MP camera, the 4-inch screen, and the A5's significantly improved graphics performance, the 5G was the first iPod touch that genuinely felt like a peer to the current iPhone rather than a generation behind.

The 5G's history is complicated by a budget variant. In May 2013, Apple quietly introduced a 16 GB model (A1509) that stripped out the rear camera, the LED flash, the wrist loop attachment, and all non-Silver colors — at $229. This model existed to fill the entry price point left by the discontinued 4th generation. It drew immediate criticism. In June 2014, Apple replaced it with a proper 16 GB A1421 model that restored the camera and all six colors at body_class: wiki-page wiki-apple 99.

The 5th generation was discontinued on July 14, 2015 with the announcement of the 6th generation. Its final software update, iOS 9.3.5, arrived August 25, 2016 — a security patch for a critical vulnerability in older 32-bit devices. iOS 10 excluded the 5G entirely, citing its 32-bit A5 processor.

data.heading: One chip jump. Four years of updates. A decade of life.

events.title: iPod touch 6G released.
events.preview: Apple A8. 8 MP camera. 1 GB RAM. Gold joins the palette. The Loop is gone.
events.body:
Apple released the 6th generation iPod touch through its online store on July 15, 2015 — the first major update to the line in more than two and a half years. It carried the 64-bit Apple A8 processor (the iPhone 6's chip), the M8 motion coprocessor, 1 GB of RAM, an 8 MP iSight camera, and 802.11ac Wi-Fi.

It launched in space gray, silver, gold, pink, blue, and (PRODUCT)RED, in 16, 32, 64, and 128 GB tiers at $199, $249, $299, and $399. The aluminum unibody and 4-inch Retina display carried over from the 5G; the pop-out Loop button did not. Apple called it "the best iPod touch yet."

events.title: Ships with iOS 8.4 and Apple Music.
events.preview: One of the first devices to carry Apple Music and Beats 1 out of the box.
events.body: The 6G shipped with iOS 8.4, released two weeks earlier on June 30, 2015. That version introduced Apple Music and the Beats 1 global radio station, making the new iPod touch one of the launch vehicles for Apple's streaming service. For a product line that began as a music player, it was a fitting pivot toward streaming.

events.title: iOS 9 — full support.
events.preview: Unlike the 32-bit 5G, the 64-bit 6G runs iOS 9 and beyond without compromise.
events.body: iOS 9 shipped in September 2015 and the 6th generation received it in full. Where the contemporary 5th generation (a 32-bit A5 device) was about to be cut off by iOS 10, the 6G's 64-bit A8 meant it had years of headroom. The device handled iOS 9's full feature set comfortably.

events.title: iOS 10 — oldest supported device.
events.preview: iOS 10 dropped all 32-bit hardware. The 6G was the oldest device to make the cut.
events.body: iOS 10 (September 2016) dropped every 32-bit device, including the 5th generation iPod touch and the iPhone 5/5c. The 6G sailed through. It was, in fact, the oldest device Apple supported on iOS 10.3 — a distinction that underlined how much longevity the 64-bit A8 had bought the line.

events.title: 16 GB and 64 GB tiers discontinued.
events.preview: Apple trims the lineup. 32 GB becomes the new floor; 128 GB the ceiling.
events.body: On July 27, 2017, Apple discontinued the 16 GB and 64 GB configurations of the 6th generation iPod touch, leaving 32 GB and 128 GB in the lineup. The move retired the cramped 16 GB base model and simplified the range to two tiers. The 6G continued on sale, unchanged, for nearly two more years.

events.title: 6th generation discontinued.
events.preview: The 7th generation arrives with an A10 chip. The 6G's nearly four-year run ends.
events.body: Apple discontinued the remaining 32 GB and 128 GB 6th generation models on May 28, 2019, with the launch of the 7th generation iPod touch. The 7G moved to the A10 Fusion processor and 2 GB of RAM, and carried the line forward to iOS 15. The 6G had been on sale for nearly four years — one of the longest single-model runs in the line.

events.title: iOS 13 — the cutoff.
events.preview: The 6G cannot run iOS 13. Feature updates end; security patches continue.
events.body: iOS 13, released in September 2019, did not support the 6th generation iPod touch — only the new A10-based 7th generation moved forward. Feature updates for the 6G ended at iOS 12. But, as with the iPhone 5s and iPhone 6 of the same vintage, Apple kept the device alive with iOS 12 security updates rather than abandoning it outright.

events.title: iOS 12.5.8 — a decade-plus of support.
events.preview: A certificate keep-alive patch, over ten years after launch. Among the longest tails in iOS.
events.body:
In late January 2026, Apple released iOS 12.5.8 for the iPhone 5s, iPhone 6, iPhone 6 Plus, several iPads, and the 6th generation iPod touch. The update extended system certificates to keep FaceTime, iMessage, and device activation working past 2027 — a 'keep-alive' patch rather than a feature release.

More than a decade after it went on sale, the 6G was still receiving code from Apple. It remains one of the longest-supported iOS devices ever made — a quiet testament to how much future-proofing the 64-bit A8 delivered in 2015.

data.heading:
What changed.
5th → 6th generation.
data.intro: The fifth-to-sixth transition was the inverse of the fourth-to-fifth one. Where the 5G had overhauled everything visible — screen, body, connector, colors — the 6G left the exterior almost untouched and poured the entire upgrade into the silicon. Same 4-inch screen, same Lightning, same aluminum unibody. But a new 64-bit A8 processor, double the RAM, a sharper camera, and faster Wi-Fi. The only thing you could see was what went missing: the Loop button.

data.heading: Six colors. Four tiers. The first 128 GB iPod touch.
intro: The sixth generation iPod touch launched with four capacities — 16, 32, 64, and 128 GB — all sharing identical hardware and all available in the full six-color palette. The 128 GB tier was the largest ever offered on an iPod touch, and the line's first move past 64 GB.

Unlike the 5th generation, there was no stripped-down budget variant. Every 6G is an A1574 with the same A8 processor, 1 GB of RAM, 8 MP camera, and Lightning connector — the only differences between units are storage and color.
